## Why it works

The whole promise is in 14 seconds: kill rats and mice "without harming any other animals" (0:01), the doubt answered ("Seems too good to be true. Well, it's not.", 0:01), then a tease that holds the method back. The next two minutes are footage and the job's back story: two companies that failed, 80 mice caught, and owners with chickens, a pig and a dog who won't use poison, which sets the safety stake. Baking soda is named at 2:11 (far later than our 15 seconds), and the promise block comes straight after: most people do it wrong (paid at 4:30 with the 2-to-1 ratio), and a professional bait that also kills fleas (paid at 11:23 and 13:36). The recipe runs as a chain of "secret ingredient" (4:45) reveals (syrup for mice, cocoa, bacon grease or tallow for rats), each with an amount, then placement along walls and why rats avoid new things. The second half is the job itself: loading the boxes, the warfarin bait and its antidote, the next-day check and a recap of the results. Blocks run about 2.5 minutes, much of it crosstalk. It ends on thanks, an email address and a comments ask with "I try to respond to all of them" (20:06). The father and daughter carry the comments (3.1K likes), and the no-poison angle drew the most-liked practical comment ("I lost a dog to a poisoned rat", 786 likes) (studies/plumbing/comparison/10-opener-teardowns.md, card 35; 11-reasons-to-stay.md).
